# Hook Generator for Reels: 50 Ready-to-Film Hooks Across 5 Niches

People who search "hook generator for reels" usually don't want another list of generic openers like "Wait for it…" or "Nobody talks about this." They want a hook for *their* Reel that they can film today. A good Reels hook needs two parts: a spoken line short enough to say in about three seconds, and on-screen text that still works when someone scrolls with the sound off. It also helps to know what kind of hook each one is, so you can test different types against each other.

Every hook below was made with the Hook Lab method. We start with a specific topic. Then we write the spoken line (about 12 words or fewer), pair it with on-screen text, and tag it with one of five types:

- **Curiosity:** opens a question the viewer wants answered.
- **Contrarian:** goes against advice they've already heard.
- **Stakes:** shows what they lose if they keep scrolling.
- **Result:** leads with the outcome.
- **Callout:** names the exact viewer it's for.

Where a hook needs a real number, you'll see `[ADD: your number]`. Put in your own figure, or rewrite the line. Never make one up.

---

## How to Choose and Test a Hook for Your Reel

A hook generator gives you options. Your job is to pick one and find out what works for your audience.

**Choose with three checks:**

- **Sound-off test:** Mute the Reel and read only the on-screen text. If it doesn't make someone curious, rewrite the text before you film.
- **Say it out loud:** Time yourself reading the spoken line. If it runs past about three seconds, cut words until it doesn't.
- **Payoff match:** The rest of the Reel has to deliver what the hook promises. A curiosity hook with a weak answer teaches viewers to skip you next time.

**Test by changing one thing at a time:**

1. Pick two hooks with *different types* for the same video idea, such as a contrarian hook and a callout hook.
2. Film the body of the Reel once. Swap only the first three seconds and the opening text.
3. Post the versions on different days, at roughly the same time of day.
4. In Instagram's Reels insights, compare how many people kept watching past the opening, not just total views.
5. Whichever *type* wins, use it for your next few Reels, then test it against a new type.

Keep notes on which hook types work for you. After a few rounds, you'll have a pattern based on your own audience instead of guesses.

## FAQ

**What makes a hook generator for Reels different from one for TikTok?**
The basics are the same, but on Reels the on-screen text carries more weight because many people watch with the sound off. A useful Reels hook generator should give you a spoken line *and* separate on-screen text, not a single sentence.

**How long should a Reels hook be?**
Aim for a spoken line of about 12 words, which fits in roughly three seconds. Keep on-screen text even shorter, ideally something people can read at a glance.

**Can I use these hooks word for word?**
Yes, as a starting point. They'll work better if you swap in your own details: your city, your client's result, your product. Any line marked `[ADD: your number]` needs a real figure from your own work.

**How many hooks should I test per video idea?**
Two is enough to learn something. Pick two different hook types, change only the opening, and compare how many people keep watching.
